e.t: Abataza, also rendered Avataza, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament text, it appears only once, in Esther 1:10. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide verse text or a further definition, its basic meaning is the name itself; the surrounding passage is needed to explain whom it identifies and what role that person has there.

Abigaia is a proper name identifying a person, rendered “Abigaia” and also associated with “Aviyea.” It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 13 times, across 13 verses, appearing in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its particular significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Greek LXX noun means “rival”: a person who stands against another in competition or opposition. It describes a relationship between opposing parties rather than an action, feeling, or quality by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX material, in 4 Maccabees 12:14. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise force of the reference must be read from that passage, but the word’s central idea remains a competing opponent.

This verb means “displace” or “put off”: to set something aside, remove it from its place, or reject it rather than accept or continue with it. It is used 60 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its central idea applies across different situations while retaining this basic sense of removal or refusal. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being displaced or put off.

This adjective means “that may be taken.” It describes a person or thing as available to be taken, rather than naming the act of taking itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs six times across Proverbs, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees, showing use in several scriptural settings. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains something that may be taken.

This noun means “delay”: a postponement or holding back that causes something to happen later. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 19:4, Nehemiah 5:13, and Ezekiel 5:3. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to a postponed action, an interval of waiting, or a deferred outcome; its central idea remains that something does not proceed immediately.

This noun means “structure,” referring generally to something built or put together. It names a constructed arrangement rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is relatively uncommon and should be understood from the sentence and surrounding passage where it appears. The word is found in passages from Genesis, 1 Samuel, Zephaniah, and Zechariah, but the available lexical meaning does not specify one particular kind of structure.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “go up,” describing movement toward a higher place or position. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The term occurs four times in the Greek LXX, in four verses across Exodus, 1 Kings, and Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains straightforward: someone or something moves upward or goes from one place to another that is higher. The surrounding verse determines the exact destination and circumstance of that upward movement.

Anoum, also given as “Anum,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 3:30. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond its function as a personal name.

Apis is a proper name, identifying a specific named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 26:15. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain the person’s role or significance; that requires the surrounding verse and passage. Thus, its basic meaning is simply the name “Apis,” preserved as a personal designation in this occurrence.

This Greek LXX adverb means “further off,” describing something located at a greater distance or positioned more remotely. It modifies a statement by indicating that a person or thing is farther away rather than nearby. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Daniel 9:7, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that verse depends on how the sentence uses this distance term.

This word is a proper name, appearing as “Ariēl” or “Aril.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, including passages in Numbers, Samuel, Chronicles, Ezra, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Because it functions as a name, its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage; the word itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this name designation.

Aroadi is a proper name, not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named biblical referent, though the available information does not specify that referent further. It occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Numbers 26:26. The related forms “Aroadi” and “Aroathi” are name renderings rather than separate ordinary meanings.

Asana is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies someone or something named Asana, but the available lexical information does not specify whether the name refers to a person, place, or another named entity. The name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 3:3 and Nehemiah 11:9. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context.

Aseriēl, also rendered Aseril, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:14. Because the available information identifies it only as a proper name and provides no surrounding verse text, its significance here is the identification of a person, not a general concept with a broader lexical definition.

Auranitis is a proper name identifying a named place in the Greek Old Testament, also rendered Avranitis. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific geographical name. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament text, both times in Ezekiel, in references to Ezekiel 47:16 and 47:18. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise geographical extent cannot be explained here, but its basic function is clear: it names Auranitis, rather than describing a person, object, or activity.

Bagadiel, also rendered Vagathil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:41. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or significance beyond identifying the name itself.

This noun refers to an “abomination”—something regarded as deeply detestable or unacceptable. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly identifies a person, practice, object, or condition viewed with strong rejection. The word occurs 117 times in the LXX corpus, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise reference—whether to conduct, worship, food, or another matter—depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains something treated as abhorrent.

Gabli, also rendered Gavli, is a proper name identifying a place or geographical location. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name preserved in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 13:5. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes its identity but does not provide further information about the location or its role in that passage.

Gadērōth, also rendered Gathiroth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 28:18. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the lexical meaning itself is the place name “Gadērōth; Gathiroth.”

Gella is a proper name, also represented as Yella. It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs once, in Joshua 21:15. The available wording preserves the name itself, so its ordinary meaning is its role as a distinctive personal or place-name; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what it identifies.

This verb means “mutter”: to speak complaints or dissatisfaction in a low, grumbling way. It describes expressed discontent rather than a simple statement or question, whether directed toward a person or a situation. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 14 times, appearing especially in passages connected with Israel’s complaints in Exodus and Numbers. Its precise force in an individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains speaking dissatisfaction aloud.

This Greek LXX noun means “genius,” naming a being or figure described by that term. Its basic meaning is stated directly, but the surrounding passage is needed to determine how the word functions in its particular setting. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Isaiah 65:11. This is an Old Testament Greek rendering, so its identity should be kept distinct from similarly rendered words in the Greek New Testament or Hebrew text.

This noun refers to the mind—the inward faculty of thought, understanding, or intention. It can describe what a person is thinking or purposefully considering, rather than an outward action alone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 63 times, appearing across the Law, historical writings, prophets, and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes thought, understanding, or intention.

This LXX Greek verb means “make quite straight” or “set right.” It describes an action that brings something into proper alignment or condition rather than leaving it crooked, disordered, or needing correction. As a verb, it expresses what someone does to straighten or restore something. It occurs seven times across Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “seat in”: it describes placing or settling someone in a seat or position. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or object. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is consistent across a small number of passages. The surrounding verse determines who is seated and the particular situation, but the word itself centers on seating or settling someone in.

This Greek LXX verb means “expel” or “cast out”: to force someone or something to leave. It describes an action of removing, driving away, or sending out rather than merely moving voluntarily. The word occurs 86 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing broad use for acts of expulsion. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on who or what is being sent away and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “draw out in battle-order,” describing the act of arranging people for an organized battle formation. It focuses on placing forces in an ordered line or deployment rather than simply gathering them together. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Numbers, 2 Kings, Daniel, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and who is being arranged for battle.

This verb means to “widen” or “extend”—to make something broader, larger, or more expansive. It can describe physical enlargement, the widening of a territory or boundary, or an increase in scope. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Amos, and Micah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being widened or extended there.

This verb means “die in,” expressing the act of dying within a particular place, situation, or condition. It describes death as occurring in or amid something rather than merely stating that someone dies. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including once in 1 Samuel and twice in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what setting or circumstance is meant in each occurrence.

This word means “there is in,” expressing that something exists or is present within a person, place, or thing. It functions as a verb in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, pointing to presence or existence rather than describing the thing itself. The word occurs 101 times in this LXX corpus, so it serves as a recurring way to state that something is found within or included in something else.

This Greek LXX verb means to snatch someone or something away from a person or place. It describes a forceful, sudden removal rather than a gentle taking. The wording focuses on separation: something is seized and carried away from its former position or possessor. This word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 7:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of abruptly taking something away from another.

This verb means “put on” or “put another.” It describes an action in which something is placed onto a person or thing, or one thing is placed onto another. As a verb, it expresses an act of putting rather than naming the object involved. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 245 times, so its exact English wording depends on what is being placed and the sentence around it. Its central idea remains deliberate placement.

Erman is a proper name identifying a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is the name itself rather than a broader concept. This form occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 14:45. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain whom or what Erman identifies there.

This Greek adjective means “red,” describing the visible color of a person, object, or place. It is a straightforward color word rather than a title, action, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 27 times, with uses spread across several books, including Exodus, Psalms, Deuteronomy, Numbers, and Joshua. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on what is being described there.

This adjective means “conspicuous”: it describes someone or something that stands out and can be readily noticed. It points to clear visibility or prominence rather than something hidden or difficult to observe. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense is being plainly noticeable.

Zeboul, also rendered Zevul, is a proper name rather than a general description or action. It identifies a named person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs six times, all within Judges 9, so its significance is tied to that narrative rather than serving as a common word used throughout Scripture. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional symbolic or descriptive meaning. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means a “spark” or “ember,” referring to a small glowing or burning piece. It names something that can remain alight after a fire or can help kindle one, while its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 8:13. The word’s basic picture is therefore a tiny but living remnant of fire.

This noun means “mule,” an animal referred to by name in the Greek Old Testament. It can identify a mule in ordinary narrative passages and lists, whether one animal or more than one. The word occurs 21 times in 19 Old Testament verses in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it names the animal itself; the surrounding verse determines what the mule is doing or why it is mentioned.

Ieththi is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 2 Chronicles 11:20. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so its particular role in that passage cannot be described here. Its meaning as a lexical entry is therefore simply the proper name “Ieththi.”

This adverb means “sufficiently” or “fully,” describing an action or condition as reaching the needed measure or degree. It can indicate that something has been done enough, or that it has been completed thoroughly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on adequacy or completeness.

Ioubal, also rendered Iuval, is a proper name for a person rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 4:21. The name itself identifies the person; its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, since a personal name does not by itself state the person’s role or importance.

This noun means “footstep”: a step made by a person’s foot. It refers to the physical act or trace of walking, depending on how it is used in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 17 times. Its central idea remains simple and concrete—a step or the mark left by one. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points more directly to the act of stepping or to a footprint.

Ιωιαδα is a proper name, rendered as “Iōiada” or “Iiatha.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both within 1 Chronicles 8:36. The available information establishes the name’s identity and use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which individual is intended or what role that person has in the passage.

This noun means “cleansing”: the act or result of being made clean. In the Greek Old Testament, it names cleansing as a recognized process rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs 18 times in the LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains cleansing or purification.

This noun means “rest”: a condition of relief, settling, or cessation from labor or movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe rest as an appointed condition or place, including the rest associated with God’s people. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with uses distributed across passages from Exodus through 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “going down,” describing something that moves or extends downward. It points to a descending direction rather than an upward one, and its exact force in a sentence depends on what it describes. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Joshua 7:5. The word’s basic sense remains a simple description of downward movement or position, without by itself expressing why something goes down or what results from it.

Kinan is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a person. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 30:28. Without the surrounding verse text, the passage does not provide enough information here to explain anything further about Kinan’s identity or role. The name itself is therefore best understood simply as a personal designation, preserved in this single occurrence.

This noun means “dung hill,” referring to a heap or mound of animal waste. It names a physical place or pile rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 15 times, showing that the word is used for this concrete object across several books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a dung heap or mound.

This verb means “carry the whole living world.” It describes bearing or supporting the entire inhabited, living order as a unified whole. The wording presents carrying as an action, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, in 4 Maccabees 15:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the act of carrying the whole living world.

This LXX noun means “lady,” referring to a woman addressed or described with respect. It can identify a woman in relation to others, as in references from Genesis, Kings, Psalms, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. The word occurs 9 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus represented here. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a female person regarded as a lady or respected woman.

Labanath is a proper name, rendered “Labanath” or “Lavanath.” As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than describing an action or quality, though the available information does not specify which. This LXX word occurs once, in Joshua 19:26. Its exact referent must therefore be identified from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name alone.

This word means “stand,” referring to an object or support that holds something up. As a noun, it names a stand rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Proverbs, where its ordinary meaning is understood through the surrounding sentence. The word itself does not necessarily describe a particular kind of stand without that context; it may refer simply to something positioned to support or hold. Its exact force in each proverb depends on the verse and its immediate wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “white,” expressing whiteness. It describes something as white rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Song of Songs 8:5. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included in this word-level entry. The English rendering also gives “white,” matching the basic lexical sense.

Maasaia, also rendered Maasea, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs seven times in seven Old Testament verses, appearing in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the same name can identify different individuals, its particular referent must be determined from the surrounding passage. As a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a person named Maasaia or Maasea.

Mardochaios, also rendered Marthokheos, is a proper name for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. This name occurs 59 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing overwhelmingly in Esther, and also once each in Ezra and Nehemiah. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This adjective describes something magnificent—lofty, splendid, and worthy of admiration. It presents a person, thing, or action as impressively great rather than ordinary or merely attractive. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Deuteronomy and three times in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence describes, but its central idea remains grandeur and splendor.

“Midday” refers to the middle part of the day, when the sun is highest or the day is at its central point. This noun names a time of day rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 26 times, showing that it is used across many passages to identify this particular time. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “measure”: to determine or express the size, amount, distance, or extent of something. It describes an action involving a standard or quantity, whether measuring a physical space, an amount received, or something’s limits. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including four Old Testament passages and one passage in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being measured, but its central idea remains making an assessment of extent or quantity.

This word means “me,” referring to the speaker or another person as the one receiving an action, being addressed, or affected by what is said. It is a pronoun, so it stands in for a person rather than naming that person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 848 times, showing that it is a common way to identify the person involved from the speaker’s or writer’s perspective. Its exact role in a sentence depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “flaw”: a defect or imperfection in something. It names what is considered defective rather than describing an action. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, beginning in Leviticus and extending as far as Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a flaw or defect.

This Greek LXX verb means “inhabit” or “dwell.” It describes living in a place or residing there, presenting habitation as an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation represented here, in Job 22:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is to live or remain in a particular place. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming the person or place involved.

This Greek LXX noun means a “cloud mass”: a visible gathering of clouds in the sky. It describes clouds as a substantial body or formation rather than as a single small vapor. The word appears 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, especially in Job. Its ordinary sense remains physical and observable, while the surrounding passage determines what the cloud is doing or what comparison is being made. It is distinct from the Greek New Testament word records.

This adjective means “of wood,” describing something whose material is wood or that is wooden. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for physical objects and materials, rather than as a name for a person or action. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Ezra, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the object it describes.

This verb means to steer—to direct or guide something toward a chosen course. It describes purposeful control rather than merely moving or drifting. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 37:10, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea remains the act of steering or directing, and the word functions as an action performed by someone or something capable of guiding a course.

This Greek LXX noun means “likeness”: a resemblance or correspondence between one thing and another. It describes something as being like, or bearing similarity to, something else rather than being identical to it. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including two occurrences in Genesis and others in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Nevertheless” is a conjunction that introduces a statement which remains true despite what was just said. It marks a contrast or qualification: one fact may point in one direction, yet the following fact still stands. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times, all in six verses among Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary function is to connect contrasting thoughts.

This word is a pronoun meaning “who” or “that,” used to identify a person or thing and connect it with what is said about it. It can introduce a description, statement, or question about someone or something, while its precise English wording depends on the sentence. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 116 times across 110 verses, appearing throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its basic function remains relational: it points to a person or thing and links that referent to an accompanying description or action.

Ophla, also rendered Ofla, is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or person; it identifies a particular location. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles and Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise geographical setting cannot be explained here, but its lexical function is clear: Ophla is a place-name preserved in these historical references.

This word describes something paradoxical—something that seems surprising or contrary to ordinary expectation—or refers to paradoxes themselves. It can function as an adjective when describing an unexpected matter, and as a noun when naming such surprising events or circumstances. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages in Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

Pachōn, also rendered Pakhon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named term in the Greek Old Testament corpus. This term occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:38. Without the verse text or wider context, its precise reference cannot be explained further here; the available lexical information establishes its identity as the name Pachōn.

This noun means a commander of fifty men, an officer responsible for a unit of that size. It identifies a leader by the number of people under his command, rather than describing a general or ruler over an entire army. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs thirteen times, showing that the term is used for a recognized level of leadership within an organized group.

This word refers to a garment—a piece of clothing or covering worn on the body. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying something as clothing rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Numbers 31:20. The word’s precise force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is simply garment.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread out; fly.” It describes movement in which something extends outward or moves through the air, functioning as an action word rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Proverbs. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains outward extension or flight. It is a concise verb for something spreading or flying.

This noun refers to the husks of corn, or bran—the coarse material separated from grain. It names the less substantial outer portion rather than the nourishing grain itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:42. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning is the husk or bran removed from harvested grain.

This noun refers to a saw or to a serrated mountain ridge—something marked by sharp, toothlike edges. Its central picture is a cutting or jagged edge, whether describing a tool or a rugged landform. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Amos. Its precise force in any one verse depends on whether the surrounding context is describing an instrument or terrain.

This noun means “stumbling.” It refers to stumbling as a recognized obstacle or failure in one’s path, whether understood literally or figuratively in a passage. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Exodus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains stumbling: encountering something that causes a person to falter or fall.

This Greek LXX verb means “spit upon.” It describes the act of spitting on or upon someone or something, functioning as an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 15:8. That reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, but the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording. Its central meaning remains direct and physical: to spit upon.

This word means “wooden tablet,” referring to a small writing surface made of wood. It is a noun used for a physical object on which words or records could be written. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four separate verses, showing a consistent reference to this kind of tablet rather than an abstract idea. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

The word means “ragged,” describing something rough, worn, torn, or shabby in appearance. It functions as a noun, identifying a person or thing by that condition rather than expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:21. The word’s basic sense is therefore narrow and concrete: it points to a ragged condition or appearance. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which gives the word its immediate context.

Samachia is a proper name, referring to a person identified by the name “Samachia,” also rendered “Samakhia.” It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) data, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 31:13. The name’s particular significance or role must be learned from that verse’s surrounding text.

Sarepta is a proper name, functioning as the name of a particular entity rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears three times, rendered consistently as “Sarepta.” Its occurrences are recorded in 1 Kings 17:9, 1 Kings 17:10, and Obadiah 1:20. The supplied information identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific role in any one passage.

This word is a proper name: “Saōn-esbi-emōēd; Saon-ezvi-emith.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 26:17. Because the available information gives the name but not its underlying meaning or the surrounding verse text, it is best understood simply as the personal designation of the individual named there, without assigning it an additional definition.
